item.title: Bainimarama applies for bail to allow him to travel to NZ for his wife's medical treatment
item.description: Suva High Court Judge Daniel Goundar will deliver his decision on Monday on former Prime Minister Voreqe Bainimarama's application to vary his bail conditions to allow him to travel to New Zealand for his wife’s medical treatment. This follows an application made by Bainimarama's lawyer, Devanesh Sharma, on 21st October, seeking permission for his client to travel overseas.
item.content:encoded:
Suva High Court Judge Daniel Goundar will deliver his decision on Monday on former Prime Minister Voreqe Bainimarama's application to vary his bail conditions to allow him to travel to New Zealand for his wife’s medical treatment.

This follows an application made by Bainimarama's lawyer, Devanesh Sharma, on 21st October, seeking permission for his client to travel overseas.

Sharma told the court that Bainimarama's wife, who has been hospitalised for almost a month and is bedridden, needs to travel to New Zealand for treatment for a spinal infection.

He said local doctors had advised that the treatment cannot be provided locally.

Sharma also told the court that Bainimarama is his wife's primary caregiver and that she has been a pillar of support for him.

He submitted that his presence would provide her with a much-needed emotional and morale boost during her treatment.

He further said that Bainimarama had never breached his bail conditions and had attended all his court cases.

Sharma said the risk of Bainimarama failing to return is minimal, adding that he did not hold a New Zealand passport or visa and is expected to return by 4th December or earlier for his court cases.

However, Assistant DPP Laisani Tabuakuro objected to the application, saying the prosecution needed to verify the medical circumstances with local doctors first.

Tabuakuro also raised concerns about the lack of proposed arrangement should Bainimarama’s wife require further treatment or an extended recovery period, which could delay the trial scheduled for December.

Judge Goundar is expected to deliver his decision on Monday in the Sigatoka Court due to a workshop in the Coral Coast.

Justice Goundar will deliver his ruling on the no case to answer involving Bainimarama, former Attorney General Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum and former Minister for Health Dr Neil Sharma on 4th December.

This is in relation to the Health Tender case.

It is alleged that Hospital Engineering and Consultancy Ltd, also known as Hospineer, was favoured in the procurement of three biomedical analysers through a waiver of the tender process instead of the recommended bidder.

Bainimarama is charged with one count of abuse of office.

Sayed-Khaiyum is charged with one count of abuse of office and one count of obstructing the course of justice.

Dr Sharma is charged with two counts of abuse of office and two counts of breach of trust by a person employed in the public service.

item.content:encoded:
The bail application for the three suspended police officers, Simione Rokosemudu, Iowane Sukanaisoro and Ilisoni Waqa, who are jointly charged in relation to the alleged murder of 24-year-old Lami Police Constable Peniasi Racagi, has been rejected by Suva High Court Judge Daniel Goundar. This is after their bail application was objected by the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

The three appeared before Justice Goundar in the Suva High Court today.

They will take their plea on November 17th.

Racagi was found dead along the Lami foreshore on February 22nd this year.

It is alleged that the three officers murdered Constable Racagi following an altercation.

item.title: Kamikamica challenges critics to identify racist provisions in proposed Constitution
item.description: The proposed Constitution is not racist, and anyone who believes it is, should identify the specific provisions, with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Industries, Commerce, Business Development, and Public Enterprises Manoa Kamikamica challenging critics to show him what is racist in the document, saying he is happy to raise any genuine concerns with the committee. Kamikamica says the propos
item.content:encoded:
The proposed Constitution is not racist, and anyone who believes it is, should identify the specific provisions, with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Industries, Commerce, Business Development, and Public Enterprises Manoa Kamikamica challenging critics to show him what is racist in the document, saying he is happy to raise any genuine concerns with the committee.

Kamikamica says the proposed Constitution is one of the fairest documents ever tabled, as it attempts to address the concerns of everyone in Fiji and bring people together .

He says Fiji has had several versions of its Constitution, and people have known for a long time what needs to change.

Kamikamica says the Constitution Review Commission consulted the public and produced its recommendations, after which the Government made its contributions before the document was tabled in Parliament.

He says the 2013 Constitution was imposed on the people of Fiji, and over the past 12 years, people have developed different views on what needs to be changed.

Kamikamica says the proposed amendments aim to address those concerns while maintaining important provisions, including national identity, equal citizenship, the Bill of Rights and issues relating to land.

He says the 2013 Constitution did not recognise chiefs and removed some of the mechanisms provided under the 1997 Constitution for iTaukei voices to be heard.

He says the proposed amendments seek to restore those mechanisms and recognition of chiefs while retaining key provisions introduced under the 2013 Constitution.

Kamikamica also points out that the role of the Bose Levu Vakaturaga in selecting the President and Vice-President was included in the 1997 Constitution.

He says this is not something new being introduced, noting that the 1997 Constitution was regarded as the best Constitution Fiji had ever had.

He acknowledges that concerns remain over immunity provisions, representation in the Senate, the role of the Bose Levu Vakaturaga in selecting the President, and the number of representatives.

However, he says these are the main issues being raised, rather than hundreds of different concerns.

On concerns about references to Christianity, Kamikamica says the proposed Constitution does not compel anyone to worship Christianity.

He says religious liberty is protected under the legislation, and the Bill of Rights makes it clear that every community in Fiji must be respected.

Kamikamica says the proposed Constitution is balanced and attempts to unify the people of Fiji.

He urges members of the public to read the document, saying it would take about half a day to go through it.

He says he is confident there is nothing racist in the proposed Constitution and challenges anyone who believes otherwise to identify the specific provisions so he can respond to their concerns.

The final parliamentary vote on the Constitution Amendment Bill will take place on November 2nd, and if it is supported by 66 percent of the Members of Parliament then Fiji will have a national referendum on December 9th.

This is where the registered voters around the country will go to the polls and have the final say on whether they are for or against the Constitution.

The new Constitution will only come into place if majority of the people who vote in the referendum support the document.

item.title: Rokoika is on medical leave receiving treatment - Tabuya responds on our fijivillage facebook page
item.description: Lavi Rokoika is on medical leave receiving treatment, and I wish her strength and recovery. That is the response by Minister for Information, Lynda Tabuya on our fijivillage facebook post regarding the whereabouts of Acting FICAC Commissioner, Lavi Rokoika.
item.content:encoded:
Lavi Rokoika is on medical leave receiving treatment, and I wish her strength and recovery.

That is the response by Minister for Information, Lynda Tabuya on our fijivillage facebook post regarding the whereabouts of Acting FICAC Commissioner, Lavi Rokoika.

There is no confirmation from FICAC and the President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, and the Judicial Services Commission on the whereabouts of Rokoika.

However we know that the JSC which has the responsibility to recommend the appointment of the FICAC Commissioner to the President is about to commence its interview process for a FICAC Commissioner after the application period closure.

Questions sent to the President and the JSC chaired by Chief Justice Salesi Temo on Rokoika remain unanswered.

Rokoika has not been in office for a few weeks now, and when we asked FICAC on who is handling the operations, no response has been sent.

The JSC had left Rokoika's appointment issue to the court after the Prime Minister appealed the High Court ruling.

fijivillage understands the JSC has not had any communication with Rokoika as they did not recommend her to the President for appointment as Acting FICAC Commissioner under the law.

Rabuka has appealed High Court Judge, Justice Dane Tuiqereqere's ruling that the dismissal of Barbara Malimali as FICAC Commissioner was unlawful, and one of the orders being sought in the appeal papers by the Prime Minister is an order preserving the status quo prior to the issuance of the judgement under appeal, including that the appointment of the Acting FICAC Commissioner Lavi Rokoika remains.

There is also a judicial review brought by Fijian and British citizen Charlie Charters against Lavi Rokoika and her illegal appointment will be called on 4th November in the Suva High Court to fix a hearing date.

Charters claims that the Prime Minister's advice and the President's appointment of Rokoika in May 2025 were unlawful and ultra vires (beyond legal authority), arguing that the recommendation power rests solely with the Judicial Services Commission after consulting the Attorney General.

When the matter was called earlier this month, Rokoika did not appear or did not instruct any lawyers.

FICAC appeared in the case and said they were representing the institution, not the Acting Commissioner.

When fijivillage News questioned Rabuka, he said the Judicial Services Commission is responsible for administering Acting FICAC Commissioner Lavi Rokoika's leave, and he does not know her current whereabouts.

item.title: Nadi and Lautoka residents urged to conserve water as dam levels decline - WAF
item.description: Residents in Nadi and Lautoka are being urged to conserve water as declining levels at Vaturu Dam put pressure on supplies during prolonged dry weather and El Niño conditions. The Water Authority of Fiji (WAF) says that as of 21st October, the dam was about 67.5 percent full, with the water level standing at 522.925 metres above sea level.
item.content:encoded:
Residents in Nadi and Lautoka are being urged to conserve water as declining levels at Vaturu Dam put pressure on supplies during prolonged dry weather and El Niño conditions.

The Water Authority of Fiji (WAF) says that as of 21st October, the dam was about 67.5 percent full, with the water level standing at 522.925 metres above sea level.

WAF says little to no rainfall in the dam’s catchment has reduced the flow of streams feeding the dam, while hot and dry conditions are increasing water loss through evaporation.

It says the falling water level is affecting the pressure and flow of raw water supplied through gravity-fed trunk mains to Nagado Water Treatment Plant.

Nagado supplies the entire Nadi system and about 70 percent of Lautoka’s water supply.

WAF says customers in elevated areas, at the ends of distribution networks and along rural offtakes on Queens Road may experience low water pressure or intermittent supply.

Affected areas may include Tavakubu, Saru Backroad, Waiyavi, Natabua, Vuda, Saweni and Kashmir in Lautoka, as well as Sabeto, Votualevu, Legalega, Nasau, Mulomulo, Korovuto and Nawaicoba in Nadi.

WAF says it may carry out controlled valve operations to help maintain reservoir levels and distribute available water across affected communities.

Some customers may experience temporary interruptions during periods of lower demand, including overnight, while reservoirs replenish to support daytime supply.

The Authority says the measures will be reviewed as conditions change, and further advice will be provided if planned water rationing becomes necessary.

With water demand already high during the hot weather and the festive season approaching, WAF is urging households, businesses and visitors to prioritise water for drinking, cooking, personal hygiene and sanitation.

People are also being asked to avoid non-essential activities such as lawn watering, vehicle washing, filling swimming pools and excessive outdoor cleaning .

WAF is encouraging customers to repair leaking taps and toilets, turn off taps when not in use and report visible leaks.

Hotels, resorts and other businesses are also being urged to review their water use in landscaping, recreation and daily operations.

The Authority says customers should keep a reasonable backup supply in clean, covered containers or suitable tanks for essential needs during possible interruptions.

WAF says its teams will continue monitoring dam levels, weather conditions, treatment plant performance and reservoir storage, while water carting trucks will remain on standby to assist affected communities during temporary disruptions, subject to operational requirements and availability.

The Authority says conserving water now could help protect supplies in the coming weeks and reduce the need for more extensive rationing if dry conditions continue.

item.title: University of Fiji looks to strengthen cultural and academic ties with Cuba
item.description: Fiji and Cuba have opportunities to strengthen their cultural and academic ties through music, arts, education and public health. This was highlighted by University of Fiji Vice-Chancellor Professor Shaista Shameem while speaking at the Cuba and Fiji Cultural Event hosted by the Cuban Embassy.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji and Cuba have opportunities to strengthen their cultural and academic ties through music, arts, education and public health.

This was highlighted by University of Fiji Vice-Chancellor Professor Shaista Shameem while speaking at the Cuba and Fiji Cultural Event hosted by the Cuban Embassy.

Shameem says the University wants to give Cuban arts and culture greater exposure in Fiji and the wider Pacific.

She says the University already has memorandums of understanding with several Cuban institutions, including the University of Havana and music production company EGREM.

Professor Shameem says these partnerships have helped maintain connections with Cuban academics and creative professionals.

She says medical education and public health are also important areas for further cooperation, building on Cuba’s contribution to the training of medical students from Fiji.

Professor Shameem says the University hopes to bring Fijian and Cuban musicians and artists together through collaborative projects and exchange programmes.

She says work is already underway to develop a musical sound combining Fijian and Cuban influences, with two recordings celebrating the countries’ musical friendship featured on a recent jazz album.

The University is also exploring the possibility of organising a music festival and bringing artists from both countries together for cultural exchanges.

Professor Shameem says Fiji and Cuba share similarities through their tropical climates, historical connections with the sugar industry, musical traditions and commitment to education.

The event also marked the launch of the Cuba-Fiji Friendship Society, which aims to encourage Fijians and Cubans to build friendships and connections within the wider community.

Cuban Ambassador to Fiji Néstor Torres says Cuba’s National Day of Culture, celebrated on 20th October each year, commemorates the first public singing of the Cuban National Anthem in 1868 during the country’s struggle for independence.

He says Cuban culture represents the unity and resilience of its people, particularly during challenging times.

Ambassador Torres says Cuba and Fiji share a strong connection with the sea, their cultural traditions and their ability to overcome adversity.

The event brought together members of the diplomatic community, academics, artists and friends of Cuba, with performances of traditional Cuban music and dance, including Guantanamera by Fijian artist Sailasa Tora.

The programme also featured a Cuban dance performance by Dalia and Osmel and an exhibition of artworks.

Those interested in joining the Cuba-Fiji Friendship Society can obtain further information from the Cuban Embassy or the University of Fiji’s Enlightenment Bookshop at its Suva Central Campus.
